name: Salvador Allende
description: Chilean president assessed through an elected socialist programme, nationalisation and institutional conflict before the 1973 coup.

axes.brief: Defended an elected constitutional road to socialism, civic freedoms and ideological pluralism.
axes.counter: Congress and courts accused his government of unconstitutional acts; supporting checks does not mean he accepted every opposition interpretation, and military overthrow was rejected.

axes.brief: Public participation, political freedoms and civil pluralism were affirmed alongside security enforcement.
axes.counter: Political polarisation and enforcement conflicts qualify absolute liberty; modern data retention and detention rules are contextual estimates, not documented opinions.

axes.brief: Cultural pluralism and Mapuche participation were supported within a Chilean national community.
axes.counter: Sovereign national development did not erase minority identity; precise modern burqa and migrant-calendar exceptions remain uncertain.

axes.brief: International solidarity and asylum traditions imply relative openness to refugees and families.
axes.counter: No complete modern migration platform is documented here; solidarity is not automatic residence for all unauthorised migrants or rejection of capacity limits.

axes.brief: Peaceful political change, diplomacy and non-intervention were emphasised with national defence retained.
axes.counter: Military capability and lawful self-defence remain compatible; nonviolent domestic socialism does not prove absolute pacifism in every foreign dispute.

axes.brief: Sovereign control of resources and resistance to foreign corporate interference were central, alongside UN cooperation.
axes.counter: International solidarity and support for common problems did not mean outside institutions could override Chilean nationalisation law.

axes.brief: Copper, banking and strategic nationalisation expanded the social-property area.
axes.counter: The programme also retained private and mixed areas; not all businesses, farms or routine services were intended to become state-owned.

axes.brief: Protected national development and resource control while contesting foreign economic pressure.
axes.counter: Foreign trade and investment were not intrinsically forbidden; strategic ownership and dependence concerns were more salient than universal tariff closure.

axes.brief: The Vuskovic programme, administered prices, nationalisation and coordinated investment strongly steered allocation.
axes.counter: Private and mixed enterprise persisted; Project Cybersyn sought feedback and coordination rather than proving all decisions were central compulsory quotas.

axes.brief: Wage increases, land reform and expanded social provision aimed to reduce deprivation and income concentration.
axes.counter: Compensation disputes and economic constraints qualify the exact compensated-land and wealth-transfer questions; outcomes are distinct from programme intent.

axes.brief: Civil constitutional government and cultural/ideological pluralism were supported without clerical veto.
axes.counter: Religious citizens and public traditions remained recognised; his personal secularism does not establish every symbolic restriction.

axes.brief: Women’s social participation and egalitarian reform challenged some inherited hierarchies.
axes.counter: The period did not establish modern same-sex marriage or gender-identity programmes; educational and family conventions remained mixed.

axes.brief: Production, healthcare, technical coordination and infrastructure were modernisation priorities.
axes.counter: Cybersyn is not direct evidence about lethal AI, embryo editing or brain implants; development enthusiasm receives cautious risk qualifiers.

axes.brief: National economic coordination coexisted with municipal participation and Mapuche-related development.
axes.counter: No regional secession or unrestricted local fiscal constitution follows from popular participation; national programmes retained central authority.

axes.brief: Social deprivation, education and economic relations were treated as changeable influences on human opportunity.
axes.counter: No exact comparative genetic account of temperament, attention or race is documented; modest estimates are explicitly contextual.
